quests.title: Evaluating Source Reliability
cards: Not everything online can be trusted. Before writing your SBA, ask: Who wrote it? When? Is there evidence?
More reliable: museum websites, university publications, artists' official websites, academic journals and official exhibition catalogues.
Be careful with: blogs with no author, social media posts, content farms and unverified AI-generated content.
Use at least two reliable sources to cross-check dates, titles and dimensions.

quiz.question: Which source is the most reliable?
quiz.explain: Museums do professional research and fact-checking.

quiz.question: Two websites give different years for a work. What should you do?
quiz.explain: Cross-checking is a basic research skill.

quiz.question: When evaluating a source, ask: who wrote it, when, and is there ____?
quiz.explain: Only information backed by evidence can be trusted.

quests.title: Citation Formats
cards: Citing respects the original author and shows your arguments are well-founded. It is part of SBA integrity.
A common format is APA: Author (Year). Title. Publisher or URL.
When citing an artwork image, write: artist, title, year, medium, dimensions, collection.
If you copy someone's sentence word for word, add quotation marks and give the source. Otherwise it is plagiarism.

quiz.question: Why should you cite sources?
options: To respect the original author and support your arguments
quiz.answer: To respect the original author and support your arguments
quiz.explain: Citing is a basic requirement of academic integrity.

quiz.question: If you copy someone's sentence word for word, you should:
options: Add quotation marks and give the source
quiz.answer: Add quotation marks and give the source
quiz.explain: Changing a few words without giving the source is still plagiarism.

quiz.question: Match the artwork information fields
quiz.explain: Complete artwork information helps readers check the facts.

quests.title: Forming a Research Question
cards: A good research question is specific, researchable and related to the theme of your art-making.
Too broad: 'What is Chinese art like?' Better: 'How does Lin Fengmian (林風眠) use square compositions to fuse Chinese and Western art?'
Start with 'How', 'Why' or 'What is the difference' to guide analysis, rather than just finding information.
Link your research question back to your own work: how do your findings shape your composition, materials or concept?

quiz.question: Which is the better research question?
options: How does Zao Wou-Ki use colour to express the mood of landscape?
How many painters are there in China?
Which painting is the most expensive?
quiz.answer: How does Zao Wou-Ki use colour to express the mood of landscape?
quiz.explain: It is specific, can be analysed and links to visual elements.

quiz.question: What is the best way to start a research question?
quiz.explain: Open-ended questions lead to deeper analysis.

quiz.question: Your research question should relate to the theme of your ____.
quiz.explain: SBA research should serve your art-making; it is not a standalone report.

quests.title: Visual Analysis with Feldman's Method
cards: Feldman's method (費德曼評賞法) has four steps: Description, Analysis, Interpretation and Judgement.
Description: say objectively what you see. Analysis: explain how elements and principles organise the picture.
Interpretation: infer meaning and emotion, supported by visual evidence.
Judgement: decide how successful the work is, with reasons, and link it to your own art-making.

quiz.question: Match the Feldman steps
quiz.explain: The four steps move from objective to subjective, going deeper each time.

quiz.question: Which step does 'The picture is mainly blue' belong to?
quiz.explain: It states the colour objectively, without judgement.

quiz.question: Which step does 'The cool palette creates loneliness, reflecting urban alienation' belong to?
quiz.explain: It infers emotion and meaning, using colour as evidence.

quiz.question: The first of Feldman's four steps is ____.
